title: A Cellar for the House
premise: Gideon Okonkwo, a third-generation pest controller who prides himself on explaining everything, is called to Marrow House to deal with 'something with fingerprints' appearing on the cellar walls. The house belonged to the late Edith Vane, whose adopted children—strangers bound only by their inheritance—each took something from the cellar in 1974 and never gave it back. As the mirrors begin lagging a second behind reality, Gideon realizes the house is not haunted but hungry: it has been keeping a ledger for fifty years, and the harvest moon is when it collects. To survive, Gideon must convince the squabbling heirs to return what they stole, discovering along the way that Edith chose them not as family but as payment—and that his own name is in her handwriting. In the end, Gideon returns the one thing no one knew was taken, himself refusing the inheritance of power Edith left him, and the heirs become the found family she never intended, burying the ledger beneath the emptied cellar.
about_author: Bram Ishikawa is the pen name of a former building inspector who spent a decade crawling through other people's basements and now writes horror about what houses remember. They live above a converted root cellar with two cats and an unreasonable number of flashlights.

chapters.title: Something With Fingerprints
chapters.summary: Gideon's POV. Called to Marrow House by a terse letter, he inspects the cellar and finds small handprints pressed into the plaster—fresh, wet, and arranged like a signature. He diagnoses moisture and mold, pockets his fee, but takes a rubbing of the prints because something about them itches at him. Emotional beat: professional skepticism curdling into unease.

chapters.title: The Heirs
chapters.summary: Gideon's POV. He returns to return a forgotten toolbox and meets the three estranged heirs: pragmatic Ruth, volatile Daniel, and silent young Theo, Edith's last foster placement. They argue over the will while the house listens; Gideon notices every clock reads 7:14, the time Edith died. Emotional beat: the comedy and cruelty of a family assembled by paperwork.

chapters.title: One Second Late
chapters.summary: Alternating POV between Gideon and Theo. Every mirror in the house begins reflecting the room a full second behind—and in that stolen second, the reflections show the cellar door open. Gideon runs experiments, timing the lag, telling himself it's a trick of light. Theo tells him plainly: the house is counting down. Emotional beat: rationality straining against evidence.

chapters.title: What Was Taken in 1974
chapters.summary: Ruth's POV, with flashback. Ruth finds Edith's ledger hidden under the kitchen floorboards: a list of names, dates, and objects—the locket Daniel pocketed, the photograph Ruth burned, the music box Theo still sleeps with. Each entry marked OWED. She realizes the fingerprints match her own child-sized hands. Emotional beat: guilt surfacing after fifty years.

chapters.title: The Ledger Keeps Itself
chapters.summary: Daniel's POV. Daniel tries to leave with the locket and finds the driveway loops back to the front gate no matter which way he drives. Inside, the walls have begun to sweat. He confesses to Gideon that Edith didn't adopt them out of love—she collected them, four children, four debts. Emotional beat: anger revealing fear.

chapters.title: Harvest Moon Rising
chapters.summary: Theo's POV. Three nights remain. The cellar stairs have grown longer overnight, and the handprints now climb toward the main floor. Theo, who loved Edith genuinely, defends her memory until Gideon shows him the final page of the ledger: a blank line bearing Theo's name and the word PAID IN FULL. Emotional beat: betrayal of the only kindness Theo ever trusted.

chapters.title: Return What Was Taken
chapters.summary: Gideon's POV. The heirs attempt restitution: Daniel buries the locket, Ruth plants a new photograph, Theo surrenders the music box. The lag shortens—but doesn't stop. Gideon rereads the ledger and understands the debts were never about objects; the house wants the taking itself undone, the choosing, the ownership. Emotional beat: hope that curdles into dread.

chapters.title: Edith's Handwriting
chapters.summary: Ruth's POV. Comparing the ledger to old letters, Ruth discovers Gideon's name written in Edith's hand decades before they met—he was the fifth child, returned to his birth mother before the debt could be collected, and the house has been waiting for him to walk back in. The mirrors now show the room a full minute late. Emotional beat: the horror of being someone else's plan.

chapters.title: The Harvest
chapters.summary: Climax, Gideon's POV. On harvest moon night the cellar opens fully and the house pulls them down into a version of 1974 where four children are being chosen. Gideon refuses the inheritance Edith offers—power over the house, over people, the corruption that made her—and instead tears out the ledger's final page, unmaking the debt. The house, given nothing to collect, begins to forget itself. Emotional beat: sacrifice as refusal, not surrender.

chapters.title: A Cellar for the House
chapters.summary: Theo's POV, epilogue. Weeks later, the mirrors run true, the clocks disagree again, and the heirs—awkward, arguing, staying anyway—begin renovating the house together. They fill the cellar with soil and plant a garden, giving the house something to grow instead of something to take. Gideon leaves, then comes back for dinner. Emotional beat: quiet, earned belonging.
